title: I automated the "which of these is better" step: an LLM art-director loop for game art
author: AnyWriting3715
selftext:
Solo dev here. I noticed my actual workflow was: generate art, paste screenshots into ChatGPT, and ask "which of these is better?", "does this fit my game?", "is it consistent with the rest?" I was using it as an art director, one paste at a time. So I automated that loop, and some of the findings surprised me, so sharing the workflow.

  
The loop:  
\- generate a batch of candidates  
\- a cheap model triages and ranks the whole batch  
\- the best image duels the current champion (both images in the same context), and it only takes over on a clear win  
\- a stronger model signs off: ship / iterate / reject, with a score and a concrete fix list  
\- the prompt is rewritten from the fix list, and the loop repeats until a "ship" survives a second blind opinion

  
Calibration turned out to be the key part. The judge never scores in a vacuum: every call carries the same fixed set of my already-shipped art as references, with an explicit note of where each sits on the scale (weakest 8.0, average 8.3, best 8.7). Without something fixed in frame, the model renormalizes to whatever it looked at last.

  
Things that surprised me:  
\- absolute scores drift between calls; pairwise duels with both images attached don't  
\- refusing "slightly better" wins stops a run from ratcheting sideways into a style nobody chose  
\- the judge is genuinely good at "which is better" and useless at "is this alpha actually clean", so I moved those checks into deterministic code outside the model  
\- a full-batch quality signal costs just 2 model calls per batch (triage + sign-off)

  
Results so far: a mobile shop screen shipped on batch 4 at 8.4/10 and got sliced into 26 individually named transparent PNGs; a one-word brief ("different emotions") became 10 consistent character sprites.

  
How do you handle QC at volume? Once a set grows past a few dozen assets, what keeps your style from drifting?

  
Full disclosure: I've been shaping this into a tool - it's called Artkiln (artkiln.dev). Both projects from this post are in a read-only demo with the full paper trail of every run, including the failed batches, no signup: https://demo.artkiln.dev/demo/the-devils-club - happy to answer anything about the judging setup.
